# Tikanipāta (AN 3)

**ID:** AN 3
**Section:** Aṅguttaranikāya (an)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Tikanipāta

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

Individual suttas of the *Tikanipāta* are frequently cited in Buddhist scholarship. Notable discourses include the *Kālāma Sutta* (AN 3.65) on epistemology and free inquiry, and the *Tittha Sutta* / *Titthāyatanādi Sutta* (AN 3.61 / 3.62), which critiques contemporary sectarian doctrines and offers an unconventional presentation of the four noble truths [Loy 2009; Shulman 2014]. In AN 3.38, the Buddha recounts his pre-awakening reflections on youth and luxury alongside the universal predicaments of old age, illness, and death [Anālayo 2017]. Other suttas discuss the three root causes of unwholesome action—greed, hatred, and delusion [Loy 2009]; three categories of persons including the "body-witness" (*kāyasakkhi*) (AN 3.21) [Radich 2007]; three types of benefactors (*bahukārā puggalā*, AN 3.24) [Collett 2014]; the right and wrong ways to observe the Uposatha explained to Visākhā (AN 3.70) [Nyanaponika, Hecker, and Bodhi 2003]; the metaphorical fragrance of virtue (AN 3.79) [Nyanaponika, Hecker, and Bodhi 2003]; and Sāriputta's counsel to Anuruddha on overcoming conceit, restlessness, and worry (AN 3.128) [Nyanaponika, Hecker, and Bodhi 2003].
